name: Vitamin E
summary: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin that protects the fats in cell membranes from damage. Real shortage is rare and mostly affects people who can't absorb fat. Large trials of vitamin E supplements didn't prevent heart disease or cancer, and some found harm.
roles: Antioxidant that protects fats in cell membranes and in blood fats (lipoproteins) from damage

status.note: The test is blood (plasma or serum) alpha-tocopherol. It rises and falls with blood fats (cholesterol and triglycerides), which carry it, so it is best read alongside them or as a ratio to them. A clearly low value (below about 12 µmol/L) points to shortage, but a normal value doesn't prove the tissues have enough. It is rarely tested except in conditions with poor fat absorption. This app has no vitamin E marker yet.

signs: Nerve damage: numbness, poor balance and coordination (ataxia), loss of the sense of where the limbs are
Damage to the retina at the back of the eye
Breakdown of red blood cells (haemolysis), mainly in premature babies
atRisk: People who absorb fat poorly: cystic fibrosis, long-standing liver or bile duct disease, Crohn's disease, short bowel, after some weight-loss operations
People with a rare inherited condition that stops the liver passing vitamin E into the blood (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, AVED)
Premature babies with very low birth weight

signs: Easy bruising and bleeding, such as nosebleeds or bleeding gums
More bleeding strokes (haemorrhagic stroke) in trials of supplements
More prostate cancer in one large trial of a synthetic supplement
More heart failure in one trial in people with heart disease or diabetes
high.note: Too much vitamin E from food isn't a known problem; EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) found that only regular users of high-dose supplements are likely to go over the upper limit. Vitamin E at high amounts thins the blood by working against vitamin K, so the risk is higher with blood thinners or a shortage of vitamin K.

examples: Vegetable oils such as wheat germ, sunflower, safflower and rapeseed oil
Nuts and seeds: almonds, hazelnuts, sunflower seeds
Spinach and other green leafy vegetables
foodSources.note: Food tables often give vitamin E as alpha-tocopherol equivalents, which also count other tocopherols, so they can show more than the alpha-tocopherol that EFSA's values refer to.

forms.name: RRR-alpha-tocopherol (natural source, 'd-alpha')
forms.note: The form found in food. The liver keeps it in the blood more readily than the synthetic form, so labels may count it as more potent per milligram. 1 IU (international unit) is 0.67 mg.

forms.name: all-rac-alpha-tocopherol (synthetic, 'dl-alpha')
forms.note: A mix of eight mirror-image forms, of which the body keeps mainly half in the blood. 1 IU is 0.45 mg. The SELECT trial used this form as the acetate.

forms.name: Esters: alpha-tocopheryl acetate or succinate
forms.note: More stable on the shelf; the gut releases the vitamin from the ester. Can be natural or synthetic, so check the 'd' or 'dl' on the label.

forms.name: Mixed tocopherols and tocotrienols
forms.note: Contain gamma-tocopherol and other related compounds. EFSA's reference values and upper limit refer to alpha-tocopherol only, the form the body keeps; the other forms are less studied.

upperLimit.note: Tolerable upper intake level (UL) for alpha-tocopherol a day from all food and supplements, for adults including pregnant and breastfeeding women. EFSA reviewed it in 2024 and kept 300 mg, with impaired blood clotting and bleeding as the key risk. It covers all forms of alpha-tocopherol, natural and synthetic. It doesn't apply to people taking blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin, people treated to prevent another heart attack or stroke, or people who absorb vitamin K poorly. The intake values are adequate intakes (AI): EFSA couldn't work out an average need, so it used typical intakes of healthy people in the EU. They are guides for groups, not personal targets.

findings.population: Healthy men aged 50 or 55 and over in the US, Canada and Puerto Rico (SELECT)
whyThisGrade: One very large, well-run randomised trial
The increase only became statistically clear with longer follow-up
An earlier trial in smokers at a lower dose (ATBC) found fewer prostate cancers, so the results aren't consistent
findings.summary: In SELECT, 35,533 men were given 400 IU a day of synthetic vitamin E, selenium, both, or placebo. With extended follow-up, the vitamin E group had 17% more prostate cancer than placebo, about 1.6 extra cases for every 1,000 men each year. Men given vitamin E with selenium had no clear increase. In ATBC (50 mg a day in male smokers) fewer prostate cancers were diagnosed, a result SELECT was partly designed to test and didn't confirm.
findings.bottomLine: In SELECT, 35,533 healthy men given 400 IU a day of synthetic vitamin E had 17% more prostate cancer than with placebo, about 1.6 extra cases per 1,000 men a year. Men given it with selenium had no clear increase.

findings.outcome: Heart attacks, strokes and deaths from heart and blood vessel disease
findings.population: Middle-aged and older adults: healthy men and women, and people with vascular disease or diabetes
whyThisGrade: Several large, long, placebo-controlled trials agree
Pooled in an independent review for the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)
findings.summary: In the Physicians' Health Study II (14,641 men, 8 years), vitamin E didn't change major heart and stroke events. In the Women's Health Study (39,876 women, 10 years) there was no overall benefit; there were fewer cardiovascular deaths, a secondary result. In HOPE-TOO (people with vascular disease or diabetes, 7 years) there was no benefit and more heart failure. The USPSTF review found no effect on cardiovascular events, and the USPSTF advises against vitamin E supplements for preventing heart disease or cancer.
findings.bottomLine: In large trials of healthy adults and of people with vascular disease or diabetes, vitamin E did not lower heart attacks or strokes overall. One trial saw more heart failure; another saw fewer heart and blood vessel deaths, but only as a secondary result.

findings.population: Adults in nine randomised trials of vitamin E, followed for at least a year
whyThisGrade: Meta-analysis of randomised trials with little difference between them
Few bleeding strokes, and the increase only just reached statistical significance
Stroke type wasn't the main outcome in most trials
findings.summary: Vitamin E didn't change the total number of strokes. But bleeding strokes (haemorrhagic) were 22% more common, about one extra for every 1,250 people taking it, while strokes from a blocked artery (ischaemic) were 10% less common, about one fewer for every 476. Bleeding strokes are usually more severe. Two large trials, PHS II and ATBC, each also saw more bleeding strokes with vitamin E.
findings.bottomLine: In nine trials, vitamin E did not change the total number of strokes, but bleeding strokes were 22% more common and strokes from a blocked artery 10% less common. Bleeding strokes are usually the more severe kind.

findings.population: Adults, healthy or with chronic diseases, in randomised trials of vitamin E alone or with other nutrients
whyThisGrade: Small effect whose size depends on which trials are included
High-dose trials were often small and done in people with chronic diseases
The independent USPSTF review found no clear difference
findings.summary: No analysis found that vitamin E helped people live longer. A Cochrane review found about 3% more deaths with vitamin E in trials at low risk of bias, at the edge of statistical significance. An earlier meta-analysis found more deaths in trials using 400 IU a day or more (about 39 extra deaths per 10,000 people) and none with lower doses. The USPSTF review, limited to healthy adults, found no clear difference. A small harm at high doses is possible but not certain.
findings.bottomLine: In trials of adults, healthy or ill, vitamin E did not help people live longer. Two analyses found slightly more deaths, one of them only at 400 IU a day or more, so a small harm at high doses is possible but not certain.

findings.outcome: Worsening of age-related macular degeneration (AMD, an eye disease that damages central vision)
findings.population: People aged about 55–80 who already have intermediate AMD
whyThisGrade: Cochrane rates the evidence moderate certainty
Most of it comes from one large trial (AREDS)
It tests a combination (vitamins C and E, beta-carotene and zinc), so vitamin E's own share is unknown
findings.summary: In AREDS (3,640 people, about 6 years), a combination containing vitamin E slowed progression to late AMD, mainly in people with intermediate AMD; for people with early AMD the absolute benefit was very small. A single trial of vitamin E alone was too small to show anything (very low certainty). Because beta-carotene in the formula raised lung cancer in former smokers, AREDS2 replaced it with lutein and zeaxanthin. This is a treatment for a diagnosed eye condition, chosen with an eye doctor, not a general prevention.
findings.bottomLine: In AREDS (3,640 people with age-related macular degeneration, about 6 years), a combination containing vitamin E slowed progression to the late stage, mainly in people with intermediate disease. It is a treatment for a diagnosed eye condition, not general prevention.

findings.outcome: Liver inflammation in fatty liver disease (NASH, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis)
findings.population: Adults without diabetes whose NASH was confirmed by liver biopsy
whyThisGrade: The outcome was a change in liver biopsy scores over 96 weeks, not liver failure or survival
Only people without diabetes were studied
findings.summary: In the PIVENS trial, 800 IU a day of vitamin E for 96 weeks improved liver biopsy findings more often than placebo (43% compared with 19%), and liver enzymes fell. It isn't known whether this prevents cirrhosis or lengthens life, and the long-term risks found in other vitamin E trials still apply. This is a treatment for a diagnosed liver disease under a doctor's care.
findings.bottomLine: In a trial of adults without diabetes whose fatty liver inflammation was confirmed by biopsy, 800 IU a day of vitamin E for 96 weeks improved liver findings more often than placebo (43% against 19%). Whether it prevents cirrhosis or lengthens life is unknown.

interactions.with: Blood thinners and antiplatelet medicines (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, clopidogrel, aspirin and others)
interactions.note: Vitamin E at high amounts makes blood clot less well and can add to the bleeding risk of these medicines. EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people taking them. Discuss any vitamin E supplement with your doctor or pharmacist.

interactions.with: Low vitamin K or poor vitamin K absorption
interactions.note: High amounts of vitamin E work against vitamin K, which the blood needs to clot. EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people who absorb vitamin K poorly.

interactions.with: A past heart attack or stroke
interactions.note: EFSA's upper limit doesn't apply to people treated to prevent another heart attack or stroke, and one trial in people with vascular disease found more heart failure with vitamin E. Ask your doctor first.
Because of the effect on clotting, tell the surgeon or dentist about vitamin E supplements before an operation.

interactions.with: Orlistat and conditions with poor fat absorption
interactions.note: Vitamin E is fat-soluble. Orlistat (a weight-loss medicine) and conditions that reduce fat absorption lower how much is absorbed. A doctor can check whether this matters.

cautions: Trial harms (bleeding strokes, prostate cancer) were seen with supplements, typically 400 IU a day or more, not with vitamin E from food.
Labels use IU or mg, and natural ('d-alpha') and synthetic ('dl-alpha') forms count differently.
Vitamin E is often added to multivitamins and 'antioxidant' products, so amounts can add up.
Unusual bruising or bleeding needs a doctor.
